solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ready for the future?

parts.note: surface reading: prepared for whatever lies ahead
setter's reading: ready is slang for cash, here savings put aside for later

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether we are prepared for what lies ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' looks like an adjective but is the noun: 'the ready' is British slang for money, so this is money kept for the future.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest egg is a sum of money saved up and kept in reserve for later years.

clue.text: The Tory won after a landslide? Remarkable!

indicators.note: a landslide tumbles everything out of place, so the letters come down in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Conservative candidate wins after a landslide election, and the result is hailed as remarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Landslide' wants to be the election result; it is what jumbles the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something noteworthy deserves attention because it stands out, a plain synonym for remarkable.

clue.text: Direction that's easy to follow

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the instruction to go ahead without turning, as two words

explanation.surface: An instruction that nobody could get wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as STRAIGHT FORWARD it is a direction to go dead ahead; as one word it means simple, so both readings share the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Straightforward describes something simple and clear, which is exactly what makes a thing easy to follow.

clue.text: Scoff all is in ruins apart from Belgium

indicators.note: 'apart from' means except, so that letter is left out of what remains

parts.note: beat-up means battered and dilapidated
B is the international vehicle code for Belgium

explanation.surface: Someone surveys a wrecked scene where everything is destroyed except Belgium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff all' is the definition, not 'Scoff': scoff is British slang for eat greedily. BEAT-UP loses its B.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat up is to consume a meal completely, leaving nothing, which is scoffing every last bit.

clue.text: Dope tires stoned groups of high people

parts.note: dope and gen are both slang for information

indicators.note: someone stoned is out of their head and in disorder, so these letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A drug-themed sentence: the dope wears out stoned groups of people who are high.
explanation.walkthrough: The drug words are all decoys: 'Dope' means information, 'stoned' scrambles, and 'high' means socially elevated.
explanation.definitionFit: The gentry are the upper class, people of high social standing, so gentries are several such ranks.

clue.text: Group in the know about attack

parts.note: a set is a group
up on, as in well informed: to be up is to be knowledgeable
on means concerning

explanation.surface: A circle of insiders who know all about a planned assault.
explanation.walkthrough: UP has the sense of well informed, as in 'up on current affairs'.
explanation.definitionFit: To set upon someone is to attack them violently and suddenly, a phrasal verb synonym.

clue.text: Sport in which runners are stood on?

definitions.text: Sport in which runners are stood on?

parts.words: Sport in which runners are stood on?
parts.note: surface reading: a race where competitors get trampled
setter's reading: runners are the long blades a sledge or skier glides on

explanation.surface: A rough athletics event where competitors get trodden underfoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runners' suggests athletes, but means the long boards that slide over snow, which the sportsperson stands on.
explanation.definitionFit: In this winter sport participants stand upon two narrow boards that glide downhill over snow.

clue.text: Inspection by nuns possibly finds guinea pig

parts.note: a test is an inspection
nuns might be described as a pious lot: PI is the crossword shorthand for pious, LOT a group

explanation.surface: A convent inspection turns up a guinea pig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuns possibly' is a description by example: a PI (pious) LOT. 'Guinea pig' is the definition, not a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: A test pilot flies new aircraft to find their flaws, serving as the experimental subject who takes the risk.

clue.text: Poor Spoonerisms fail to display this

definitions.text: Poor Spoonerisms fail to display this

indicators.note: poor work is botched, so these letters are badly put together and must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A speaker who garbles words in clumsy swaps shows a lack of polish.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: mixing up 'Spoonerisms fail' yields what such slips lack. A Spoonerism swaps initial sounds of words.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip of the tongue betrays a lack of the polished competence expected of an expert performer.

clue.text: London hospital making good northern grub

indicators.note: 'making X Y' turns one thing into another, so one letter becomes a different one

parts.note: Great Ormond Street Hospital, a famous children's hospital in London
G is the abbreviation for good
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A hospital in the capital serving decent food from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: GOSH has its G (good) turned into N (northern). Nosh is British slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Both grub and nosh are informal slang words meaning food or a meal.

clue.text: Top player first to be sent off pitch

indicators.note: the opening letter is dismissed, so it is dropped from the word

parts.note: a star is a leading performer

explanation.surface: A football star is shown a red card and sent off the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent off' and 'pitch' make a football scene, but pitch is the black sticky substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitch is a dark resinous substance made from coal or wood, a close synonym for that black road coating.

clue.text: Server wear seen in hosts needs fixing

indicators.note: something needing repair is broken, and its letters must be reassembled into a working order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A computing complaint: wear on servers spotted in the hosts needs repair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Server' and 'hosts' suggest computers, but the server is a tennis player.
explanation.definitionFit: A server in tennis puts the ball into play, and players wear special shoes on court.

clue.text: Scamp dashes to net a kipper

indicators.note: to net something is to catch it inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: whips means moves quickly, dashes
a as in 'five pounds a head', meaning per
someone who kips is a sleeper, one who naps

explanation.surface: A mischievous child rushes off to catch a smoked herring in a net.
explanation.walkthrough: A kipper is a smoked herring, but here it is someone who kips (British slang for sleeps).
explanation.definitionFit: A whippersnapper is a cheeky, presumptuous young person, much like a mischievous rascal.

clue.text: Improvised performance in WI event?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: musicians playing together unrehearsed
second meaning, playful: a meeting spent making fruit preserves

explanation.surface: Someone ad-libbing a turn at a Women's Institute gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: The WI is the Women's Institute, a British women's organisation famous for making jam, so its gathering could whimsically be a session of jam.
explanation.definitionFit: Musicians meet to play freely without rehearsal; the second reading pictures a preserves-making meeting.

clue.text: Grass arresting officers abroad grilled again?

indicators.note: arresting someone means seizing and holding them, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass
'the heat' is American slang for the police

explanation.surface: An informer turns in foreign police, who are then interrogated a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' looks like British slang for an informer and 'grilled' like questioning; both are decoys.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has been grilled a second time has been warmed up once more, with the question mark flagging the pun.

clue.text: A department head might have it

definitions.text: A department head might have it

parts.note: taken as written
DEPT is the standard abbreviation
a ness is a headland, a promontory

explanation.surface: A manager in charge of a department is likely to possess a certain quality.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the parts spell the answer, and the sentence describes a skill a manager might have. 'Head' is a headland, not a boss.
explanation.definitionFit: Adeptness is skill and proficiency, the competence one hopes a senior manager possesses.

clue.text: A question and answer about liberal state

indicators.note: about means around, so these letters go round another

parts.note: taken as written
to ask is to question
A is the abbreviation for answer
L is the abbreviation for liberal

explanation.surface: A Q&A session about a progressive political position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal state' reads as a political phrase, but the state is American and 'liberal' supplies one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Alaska is one of the fifty American states, the largest by area, an example of the definition.

clue.text: Bit of backbone shown by green energy supporter

parts.note: vert is the heraldic word for green
E is the symbol for energy
a bra is a supporting undergarment

explanation.surface: An environmental campaigner backing renewable power shows some courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green energy supporter' reads as an eco activist; it splits into three separate parts.
explanation.definitionFit: The spine is made up of a column of small bones, each one a single segment of the spinal column.

clue.text: Delighted benches Conservative angered

indicators.note: a team that benches a player leaves them out of the side, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: chuffed is British slang for pleased
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A happy figure takes a seat while an irritated Tory looks on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Benches' suggests Parliament's seats alongside 'Conservative', but here it means dropping a player.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in a huff is sulking with annoyance, so huffed means made irritated or offended.

clue.text: Plant training volunteers around Stirling?

parts.note: PE is physical education

indicators.note: turned around means facing the opposite way, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: the TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force
Stirling Moss was a famous British racing driver

explanation.surface: A training plant where volunteers gather near the Scottish town of Stirling.
explanation.walkthrough: Stirling looks like the Scottish town; it is the first name of Stirling Moss, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Peat moss is sphagnum, a bog-growing vegetation used by gardeners in compost.

clue.text: When coming across inspiration is funny

indicators.note: something coming across another spans it from side to side, so it wraps around it

parts.note: as means when, as in 'as I left'
a muse is a source of artistic inspiration

explanation.surface: A remark that finding a flash of creative insight is comical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming across' looks like discovering something; here it means spanning around another piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that amuses makes people laugh or smile, which is what being comical does.

clue.text: Am I certain this dispersed adders?

indicators.note: things dispersed are scattered about, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone nervously asking whether they really scattered a nest of venomous snakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adders' looks like snakes but means people who add up figures.
explanation.definitionFit: Mathematicians who work with numbers, especially sums, are people who add up figures.

clue.text: Church split by concerning democratic dogma

indicators.note: a thing split by something has that thing driven into its middle, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
re means about, concerning
D is the abbreviation for democratic

explanation.surface: A church divided over a doctrine about democracy.
explanation.walkthrough: CE is the standard abbreviation for the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A creed is a set of religious beliefs or principles, closely synonymous with a doctrine or dogma.

clue.text: Piece of paper?

parts.note: surface reading: a scrap or sheet torn off
setter's reading: a newspaper, and a piece in it is a single news report

explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of paper' suggests a sheet; the paper is a newspaper and the piece is a story printed in it.
explanation.definitionFit: An individual article or report in a newspaper is called a news story, or simply one entry.

clue.text: Passable food tucked into by partygoers

indicators.note: a meal tucked into has eaters getting stuck right in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: table means the food served, as in 'keeps a good table'
ravers are people who go to wild parties

explanation.surface: A reviewer finds the spread at a party, eaten heartily by the guests, merely acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passable' looks like a verdict on the food; it means able to be crossed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground that is traversable can be crossed or travelled over, so it is passable.

clue.text: Tribe discovered in Thai wilderness

indicators.note: something discovered within has been found lying inside, so the letters are tucked in the words that follow

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: An explorer comes across a remote people living in the Thai jungle.
explanation.walkthrough: The tribe is not Thai at all: iwi is the Maori word for a tribe in New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: Iwi is the Maori term for a people or large tribal grouping in New Zealand society.

clue.text: Petrifying women in America involved in drugs

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be wrapped up within it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: meds is short for medications
USA is the abbreviation for America

explanation.surface: Terrifying American women caught up in the narcotics trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Petrifying' means terrifying in the surface but literally turning to stone: in Greek myth the Gorgon's gaze did this.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gorgon of myth turned onlookers to stone, so fearsome females of that kind literally petrify.

clue.text: Where corporation is in bother over British boys

indicators.note: something laid over another covers it, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: ado is fuss or bother
B is the abbreviation for British
boys, as in 'one of the boys', means men

explanation.surface: A company in trouble with some young British employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a company, but it is old British slang for a pot belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A paunch sits on the belly, the lower front part of the trunk containing the stomach.
